newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - S&P raises HK, China ratings.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - S&P raises HK, China ratings.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp gave China and Hong Kong credits a modest boost on Wednesday by announcing it had upgraded the two entities' ratings.
S&P raised China's sovereign rating to BBB-plus from BBB, citing the country's progress in economic reforms, its strong economy and its considerable external financial flexibility.
Hong Kong's long-term foreign currency rating was raised to A-plus from single-A, while its long-term local currency rating was upgraded to AA-minus from A-plus.
Hong Kong's upgrade was based on the improvement in China's ratings, S&P said.

Unlike rival rating agency Moody's Investors Service, which rates Hong Kong and China equally at A3, S&P has long maintained that Hong Kong and China will remain separate enough after the transfer of sovereignty to merit separate ratings.
"As long as there is a significant difference between Hong Kong and China, we would expect there to be a gap in ratings," said Paul Coughlin, managing director at S&P in Hong Kong.
S&P said today that the key factors underpinning the three-notch rating differential with China remain firmly in place as the transfer of sovereignty nears.
"China's incentives to respect Hong Kong's autonomy will continue to be strong, especially as economic reforms in the mainland deepen," S&P said in a statement.
Stephen Taran, research director at Lehman Brothers, said that by rating China and Hong Kong separately, S&P is saying that it believes Hong Kong's automony will be "rock solid" after the handover.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Traders in Hong Kong said the rating action should give a boost to Hong Kong and China credits traded in the secondary market.
They said this would be the case, even though China credits already tend to trade closer to single-A credits than triple-B.
In addition to raising the sovereign ratings, S&P raised State Development Bank of China to BBB-plus from BBB. It also raised the ratings of a number of top-rated Hong Kong firms.
Traders said they expected SDB to benefit most from the rating action because its outstanding bonds have been trading wide of the sovereign benchmark.
SDB's bonds due in 2007 tightened 2-3 basis points after the rating action to about 86-89 basis points over the benchmark, they said.
China's sovereign issue due 2006 reportedly is trading at about 82 basis points over Treasuries.

China issues have tightened significantly over the last year -- the China global bond was launched at 110 basis points over Treasuries when it launched in July 1996 -- but spreads have widened several basis points over the last couple of months along with declines in other emerging debt.
The ratings upgrade may give China added incentive to launch another bond soon. Bankers said the PRC has been eyeing the market for some time without making any firm commitments.

Other Chinese banks that had been rated equally with the sovereign -- Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China International Trust and Investment Corp and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China -- will not be upgraded to BBB-plus because they are becoming more commercialized and can no longer be considered sovereign credits, Coughlin said, reiterating comments made by S&P in March.
The rating agency in March had affirmed the ratings of these banks at BBB and revised their outlooks to stable from positive.
